topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Memory defects often appear far from their cause. Instrumented builds can turn a silent overwrite or invalid lifetime access into a diagnostic closer to the offending operation. This chapter pairs a correct bounded buffer with an explicitly isolated negative example; the unsafe program is excluded from ordinary builds and must never be counted as a passing functional test merely because it terminates.

topics.title: 10.1.1 Detecting Invalid Memory Access
topics.summary: AddressSanitizer instruments supported memory operations and manages runtime metadata to detect classes such as out-of-bounds accesses and use-after-free. Build and link the relevant code with compatible instrumentation so the runtime is available. Its diagnostics identify observed violations, not every possible memory error in unexecuted paths.

topics.title: 10.2.1 Identifying Leaked Allocations
topics.summary: A leak occurs when a resource remains allocated after its ownership should have ended. Heap leak detectors can report certain unreachable allocations at process termination, but a still-reachable unbounded cache can exhaust memory without matching that narrow definition. Track both ownership correctness and application-level growth.

topics.title: 10.2.2 Tracking Resource Ownership
topics.summary: RAII makes ordinary cleanup follow object lifetime, reducing the number of paths that need manual release code. A move-only owner expresses transfer; a raw pointer or span normally borrows. Review any escape of a borrowed view beyond the owner’s lifetime, even when no explicit delete appears nearby.

topics.title: Turning Ownership into RAII to Eliminate a Leak Path
topics.summary: Leak detection is most useful when it leads back to an ownership defect. This contrasts manual allocation whose cleanup is skipped during an exception with RAII ownership that cleans up during unwinding.

  source/book05/ch10/optional/unsafe.cpp -o build/unsafe-asan
ASAN_OPTIONS=halt_on_error=1 build/unsafe-asan 8
